title: FlashAttention / Paged / FusedOps interaction matrix and experiments
body:
Purpose:
Quick capture of a set of experiments trying to map interaction effects between FlashAttention (FA), paged attention, and fused ops. Goal is to find robust config regions where latency SLOs (p50/p95) are stable while preserving throughput and avoiding kernel handoffs that spike tail latency.

Short summary of result (TL;DR):
- There are clear 2-way and 3-way interaction effects: enabling fused ops reduces p50 in steady-state, but in mixed-seq workloads it increases p95 when combined with aggressive prefetch (high prefetch density) and small page sizes.
- FlashAttention kernel switch thresholds (seq_len and batch thresholds) are a strong lever — moving the FA switch to prefer FA earlier reduces p50 but can increase kv-cache contention on long-history workloads causing p95 spikes.
- Paged attention reduces peak memory pressure for very long context but creates a sensitivity to prefetch density; if prefetch_density is too low we see IO stalls, if too high we see kernel aborts due to buffer churn.

Experiment matrix (high-level):
- Variables swept:
  - prefetch_density: {0.1, 0.5, 0.9} (fraction of pages prefetched ahead)
  - page_size_kb: {64, 256, 1024} (page size in KB for paged attention)
  - fused_ops: {off, on} (enable fused matmul/softmax kernels)
  - flash_switch: {conservative, default, eager} (when runtime chooses FA vs paged/flashed fallback)
  - workload_mix: {uniform-short, mixed, long-history-heavy} (sequence length distributions)
  - batch_shapes: {(32x128), (8x512), (4x2048)} (batch x seq_len)

- Measurement axes collected per run:
  - tokens/sec (aggregate throughput)
  - p50 latency (ms) and p95 latency (ms)
  - GPU util (avg), GPU memory usage (peak)
  - kernel-switch-counts (how many times runtime switched kernel types per interval)
  - fallback_rate (percent of requests that hit fallback non-FA path)

Representative table (trimmed):
Run | prefetch | page_kb | fused | flash_switch | workload | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | tps | fallback %
-----|----------|---------|-------|--------------|----------|---------|--------|-----|---------
A1 | 0.1 | 256 | on | default | mixed | 23 | 98 | 4800 | 12
A2 | 0.9 | 256 | on | default | mixed | 19 | 210 | 5100 | 34  <-- observed kernel aborts, tail spikes
B1 | 0.5 | 64  | off | eager   | long-history-heavy | 45 | 320 | 1400 | 8
B2 | 0.5 | 1024| on  | conservative | mixed | 28 | 110 | 3700 | 3
C1 | 0.1 | 256 | on | eager | uniform-short | 12 | 20 | 12000 | 0

Key observations and hypotheses:
1) Prefetch density sweet spot is workload dependent. Mixed workloads (short bursts with occasional long history) suffer when prefetch_density is too high: the runtime aggressively pulls pages for long sequences, disrupting coalesced small-batch execution and causing fused kernels to abort and fall back mid-exec. Hypothesis: page churn causes allocator pressure + kernel handshake timeout.

2) Small page sizes (64KB) reduce memory pressure but increase I/O ops for long-history sequences; combined with fused_ops the scheduler attempts to keep kernels fused and stalls on missing pages leading to big p95 hits.

3) Eager FlashAttention switching helps short/medium sequences but on long-history-heavy workloads it reduces the effectiveness of KV cache sharing (we observe more unique KV pages touched), increasing memory bandwidth and causing p95 regressions.

4) Fused ops give consistent p50 wins for steady shapes (uniform short or predictable batches). However, in bursty mixed-seq traffic fused ops amplify scheduling noise because fused kernels are less preemptible and their preparation cost is higher — leading to a larger tail when something causes them to abort.

Trace-level signals to watch (what to add to runtime telemetry):
- page-prefetch-latency histogram (per-request)
- fused-kernel-abort-reason tags (OOM, missing-page, handshake-timeout)
- per-request kernel choice timeline (sequence of kernel types with timestamps)
- allocator-evict-counts and page-revive counts (detect churn)
- kv-page-hotness (how many requests hit same page id)

Repro recipe (how we ran A2 which showed bad tail spikes):
1) Single-GPU p4d (experimental test cluster) with default CUDA streams and on-device allocator.
2) Model: Llama-like 13B quantized FP16/INT8 hybrid; KV cache configured to keep last 10240 tokens when paged.
3) Traffic: synthetic mixed workload generator (90% reqs seq_len 128, 8% seq_len 1024, 2% seq_len 4096) at load ~70% target throughput.
4) Runtime config: fused_ops=on, page_size=256KB, prefetch_density=0.9, flash_switch=default.
5) Capture: perfetto traces, runtime logs, and GPU nsys for 30 minutes.

Interesting trace snippet (human-readable):
- Time 00:12:03.133: request_47 enters, scheduler assigns fused kernel; prefetch kicks for 4096-history pages (7 pages).
- 00:12:03.145: page request for page_3 delayed 8ms due to evict-reclaim. fused kernel handshake waits and times out -> abort -> fallback to paged scalar path.
- 00:12:03.149: request_47 completes on fallback with 110ms additional latency; concurrent fused kernel initiation for request_49 blocked on same allocator lock -> p95 spike cluster.

Notes to self / discussion questions:
- Can we make fused kernels more tolerant to missing pages (deferred soft-fail) instead of hard abort? Potential small change in fused operator interface to accept partial pages and proceed with on-demand copies.
- Investigate allocator policy: current LRU eviction knob might be too aggressive when prefetch_density>=0.8. Maybe switch to a reservation-based prefetch throttle per-request.
- Is it worth adding per-request prefetch-level hints in API so callers that expect long-history can mark requests long-history and get higher reservation?
- Need to quantify the cost of smaller page sizes in terms of CPU overhead (more page ops) vs. memory/regression lowering for mixed traffic.

Actionable next steps (short term):
- [ ] Add fused-kernel-abort-reason to telemetry (owner: Priya).
- [ ] Run a narrower sweep with page_size fixed to 256 and prefetch_density in 0.2 steps (0.2..0.9) to find operational sweet spot for mixed workloads (owner: Michael).
- [ ] Prototype a deferred-fallback path where fused kernel can operate on partial pages with zero-copy fallback for missing regions (owner: Lucas).
- [ ] Add a dashboard showing kernel-switch-counts correlated with p95 and prefetch_density (owner: Observability team).

Longer term ideas:
- Automatic per-customer prefetch policy based on observed seq_len distribution. Use a small online model to set prefetch_density dynamically per-queue.
- Smarter allocator that can pin pages for high-priority requests or reserve a working set for fused ops to avoid handshake timeouts.
- Evaluate hybrid page sizes (adaptive page sharding where long-history pages use 1MB pages and short-history use 64KB) — complexity tradeoff but potentially large wins.

Unresolved questions / TODOs:
- Need to validate behavior on A100 vs p4d GPUs (memory subsystem differences). We ran primarily on p4d; does A100 show the same abort pattern?
- Confirm whether kernel aborts recorded are actually caused by missing pages vs. stream synchronization issues. Some traces show handshake-timeouts with no obvious page evict in logs. Might need to widen trace scope.

Appendix: quick perf checklist for repeated runs
- Clear GPU allocator/host caches between runs (script in tests/perf/clear_state.sh)
- Ensure deterministic synthetic generator seed
- Collect: perfetto, nsys, runtime logs (level=debug), and allocator histograms

References and related artifacts:
- PR with initial fused partial-fail sketch: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/5123
- Related Jira: JIRA-RT-789 (paged-attn prefetch throttling epic)
- Slack thread: #eng-serving-runtime (see pinned message from 2024-10-29)

Bottom line: there isn't a single "flip a knob" fix. The system exhibits complex interactions: fused kernels improve steady p50 but are fragile in page-churned mixed workloads. We should invest in better telemetry + small runtime changes (deferred-fallback + allocator reservations) and a targeted config sweep to identify operational sweet spots for our common traffic mixes.
